title: Golden West Airlines 261

aircraft.type: de Havilland Canada DHC-6 Twin Otter

summary: A Golden West Airlines de Havilland Canada DHC-6 Twin Otter collided with a Cessna 150 near Whittier, California on January 9, 1975 at 4:07 p.m. PST. The sun was positioned only 9 degrees above the western horizon, directly in the line of sight of the pilots of both aircraft. Neither flight crew saw the other aircraft in time to initiate evasive action and no avoidance maneuvers were attempted.
probable_cause: The failure of both flightcrews to see the other aircraft in sufficient time to initiate evasive action, with reduced visibility due to sun position, closure angle, and difficulty acquiring radar-reported traffic.

factors.evidence: the Cessna's firewall and instrument panel were embedded in the Twin Otter's fuselage forward of the wing

The Cessna impacted the left side of the Twin Otter at an approximate angle of 90 degrees

title: 1975 Kjalarnes helicopter crash
summary: A Sikorsky S-55B helicopter en route from Reykjavik Airport to Snaefellsnes crashed by the Hjardarnes farm in Hvalfjordur, Iceland, on January 17, 1975. The helicopter was carrying two crew members and five employees of RARIK, the Icelandic State Electricity company. The cause was wind conditions at Hjardarnes; the aircraft was also believed to have been overloaded. All seven occupants were killed on impact, making it the deadliest helicopter crash in Icelandic aviation history.
probable_cause: The cause of the crash was wind conditions at Hjardarnes. The helicopter was also believed to have been overloaded but the investigative committee stated that the crash would have likely occurred even if it had been correctly loaded.

title: 1975 Royal Nepal Airlines Pilatus PC-6 Porter crash
summary: A Pilatus PC-6 Porter chartered by Sir Edmund Hillary crashed on 31 March 1975 shortly after takeoff from Tribhuvan International Airport in Kathmandu. All five occupants, including the pilot and Hillary's wife and daughter, were killed. An investigation later found that a ground-locking pin on an aileron was not removed before flight, which the pilot failed to detect because he did not perform a pre-flight walk-around due to being late.

title: 1975 Tan Son Nhut C-5 accident
summary: A C-5A Galaxy departed Tan Son Nhut at 16:15 heading for Clark Air Base. At 4:15 p.m. while climbing to 23000 ft over the South China Sea 13 nm off Vung Tau, the locks on the rear loading ramp failed and the cargo door opened explosively. The explosive decompression severed control cables to the tail and caused two of four hydraulic systems to fail, leaving only one aileron and spoilers. The crew performed a 180-degree turn to return to Tan Son Nhut, countering phugoid oscillations during descent. At 16:45 during final approach the descent rate increased and despite engine thrust the aircraft touched down in a rice paddy and broke up.
probable_cause: Failure of cargo door locks from inadequate maintenance combined with loss of flight control authority during approach.

title: Agadir air disaster
summary: A Royal Air Maroc Boeing 707 flight from Paris to Agadir crashed into a mountain on August 3, 1975 while descending to land at Inezgane Airport. The aircraft was flying over the Atlas Mountains in heavy fog. The right wingtip and number 4 engine struck a peak about 45 miles northeast of Agadir at 2400 feet altitude. The aircraft lost control and crashed into a valley. All 188 passengers and crew aboard were killed, making it the deadliest crash involving a Boeing 707.
probable_cause: The cause of the crash was determined to be pilot error in not ensuring positive course guidance before beginning descent. The aircraft had not followed the usual north-south corridor generally used for flights to Agadir and was flying from the northeast over the Atlas Mountains.

title: Overseas National Airways 032
summary: During takeoff roll at approximately 100 knots, a large flock of gulls rose from the runway directly in front of the DC-10. Bird ingestion into the right engine caused an uncontained engine failure that ruptured landing gear tires, disabled the number 2 hydraulic system which powers the number 3 engine, and partially disabled spoilers and landing gear brakes. The crew initiated a rejected takeoff but the aircraft did not decelerate normally, veered left toward a taxiway, and ran off the runway. The aircraft was destroyed by intense post-crash fire with all 139 occupants surviving.

title: Graham Hill plane crash
summary: Former Formula One champion Graham Hill's Piper Aztec crashed near Arkley in the London Borough of Barnet on November 29, 1975 during a nighttime approach to Elstree Airfield in thick fog with visibility 50 to 100 metres. The aircraft descended from 1500 feet below which descent was pilot's discretion, then lost radar contact with London Approach. The investigation found the aircraft unregistered and stateless, the pilot's night flying and instrument flying ratings had expired, and the most likely cause was the pilot mistaking the lights of Barnet for Borehamwood and the Arkley Golf Course for the dark area next to Elstree airfield, leading to premature descent into terrain.
probable_cause: Pilot error during approach in low visibility conditions, descending the aircraft prematurely due to misidentification of ground features and lights.

title: Cashel South African Air Force Alouette crash

location.name: Shinda Orchards Farm near Cashel, 3 km from Mozambican border

summary: An Aérospatiale Alouette III helicopter of the South African Air Force carrying two crew and four Rhodesian Army officers crashed on December 23, 1975, near Cashel in Rhodesia. Flying at low altitude in accordance with counter-insurgency procedure, the helicopter collided with a rusty, long-forgotten hawser cable that had years before been used to pass logs down a steep slope. The cable was unmarked on any maps. The airframe broke up as the helicopter spun out of control and crashed. Five occupants were killed and the pilot was severely injured, losing one leg.
probable_cause: The helicopter flying at low altitude struck an unmarked hawser cable near Cashel during a routine counter-insurgency mission. The cable, which had been used years before to pass logs down a slope, was not charted on any maps. Upon impact with the cable, the airframe began to break up as the helicopter spun out of control and crashed.
